title: Isoflavone supplementation influenced levels of triglyceride and luteunizing hormone in Korean postmenopausal women.
text_summary: 本研究旨在评估大豆异黄酮对韩国绝经后女性血糖、血脂和与心血管疾病相关的性激素水平的影响。通过双盲、随机、安慰剂对照试验，选取85名绝经后女性，每日服用70毫克异黄酮或安慰剂胶囊12周。结果显示，与安慰剂组相比，治疗组的甘油三酯（TG）水平显著降低（p = 0.0215），促黄体生成素（LH）水平也显著降低（p = 0.027），而促卵泡激素（FSH）、雌酮和雌二醇水平则没有变化。研究结果表明，每日70毫克异黄酮补充12周可降低韩国绝经后女性的TG和LH水平。
text:
RESEARCH ARTICLE
Isoﬂavone supplementation inﬂuenced levels of triglyceride
and luteunizing hormone in Korean postmenopausal women
Jinkyung Kim • Hansongyi Lee • Okhwa Lee •
Kyun-Hee Lee • Yoon-Bok Lee • Kwon Dae Young •
Yang Hye Jeong • Ryowon Choue
Received: 31 May 2012 / Accepted: 5 December 2012 / Published online: 10 March 2013
 The Pharmaceutical Society of Korea 2013
Abstract
We conducted a double-blind, randomized,
placebo-controlled trial to evaluate the effects of soy-
derived isoﬂavone on blood glucose, lipid proﬁles, and sex
hormones related to cardiovascular disease in Korean
postmenopausal women. One hundred thirteen postmeno-
pausal women were recruited from the Seoul metropolitan
area. To conﬁrm postmenopausal and gynecologic status,
the subjects were clinically examined by a gynecologist
using ultra sound and X-ray. Finally, 85 postmenopausal
women whose follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) levels
were
higher
than
40 IU/ml
were
enrolled.
Subjects
received either 70 mg isoﬂavone or placebo capsules daily
for 12 weeks. As a result, the values of fasting glucose,
insulin and HOMA-IR, as well as those of TC, LDL-C,
HDL-C and FFA, were not different between the groups
after supplementation. However, triglyceride (TG) levels in
the treatment group decreased signiﬁcantly compared with
those of the placebo group (p = 0.0215). The levels of
luteinizing hormone (LH) signiﬁcantly decreased in the
treatment group (p = 0.027); however, the levels of FSH,
estrone and estradiol were not changed after intervention.
In conclusion, isoﬂavone supplement of 70 mg/day for
12 weeks decreased blood levels of TG and LH in Korean
postmenopausal women.
Keywords
Postmenopausal women  Isoﬂavone  Lipid
proﬁles  Sex hormones  Korean
Introduction
Menopause is a risk factor for cardiovascular disease
(CVD) because estrogen deﬁciency has unfavorable effects
on body composition, insulin metabolism, and lipid proﬁles
(Rosano et al. 2007). These suggested that endogenous
estrogen production may play a key role in CVD (Vitale
et al. 2010). It has been hypothesized that estrogen therapy
delays the condition of CVD in postmenopausal women.
However, the effects of exogenous estrogen are not well-
established in clinical research ﬁndings. The Women’s
Health Initiative (WHI) found that, although calciﬁed-
plaque was lower in the estrogen therapy group than in the
placebo group (WHI and WHI-CACS investigators 2007),
the risk of CVD and stroke increased in postmenopausal
women with oral administration of estrogen (WHI inves-
tigators 2002; WHI Steering Committee 2004). As such, it
is important to ﬁnd safe strategies for protection against
CVD in postmenopausal women.
Subsequently, many well-controlled studies explored
the soybean hypothesis on the biomarkers related to CVD;
it has been recognized that soy product contains bioactive
molecules called isoﬂavones (Sacks et al. 2006). Soy
contains three primary isoﬂavones in glycoside form,
genistin, daidzin, and glycitin. These primary forms have

a sugar removed during digestion by b-glycosidases,
resulting in the formation of aglycone, genistein, daidzein
and glycitein. These compounds then act via estrogen
receptor binding (Usui 2006). Because these compounds
have weak estrogenic action (Sacks et al. 2006), soy
isoﬂavones have been hypothesized to improve several
estrogen-dependent conditions in postmenopausal women.
Thus, researchers have studied the effects of isoﬂavone on
menopausal symptoms such as hot ﬂash. Although there
have been a few studies looking at the relationship
between isoﬂavones and cardiovascular biomarkers in
Asian or Korean postmenopausal women, the effects of
isoﬂavone on cardiovascular biomarkers remain uncertain.
In this study, we evaluated the effects of soy-derived
isoﬂavone supplementation on glucose, lipid proﬁles, and
sex hormones related to CVD in Korean postmenopausal
women.
Materials and methods
Subjects
One hundred thirteen postmenopausal women from the
Seoul metropolitan area were recruited through posters and
through community center visits from March to November
2010. The ﬁrst criterion for eligibility was that these
women
experienced
their
last
menstruation
at
least
12 months prior to the beginning of the study. The women
who received hormone replacement therapy (androgen,
estrogen, progesterone, and respectively related synthetic
drugs) or who take medication (selective serotonin reup-
take inhibitors, such as escitalopram oxalate, ﬂuoxetine
hydrochloride, ﬂuvoxamine maleate, paroxetine hydro-
chloride, paroxetine, sertraline hydrochloride) or health
functional foods containing isoﬂavones or sophoricosides,
known to inﬂuence estrogen levels were excluded. The
subjects who were menopausal due to hysterectomy, had a
history of cancer within 5 years, liver and kidney diseases
or thyroid disorder, or who had an allergy to soy-beans
were also excluded. Furthermore, subjects with fasting
blood glucose and blood pressure above 180 mg/dl and
170/100 mmHg, respectively, were excluded. To conﬁrm
postmenopausal status, gynecologic problems, and breast
condition, the subjects were clinically examined by a
gynecologist. Finally, the subjects with a follicle stimu-
lating hormone (FSH) level exceeding 40 mIU/ml were
enrolled. All subjects provided written informed consent
for participation in the study. The research protocol was
approved by the Institutional Review Board (KMC IRB
1002-02) of Kyung Hee University Medical Center (Seoul,
Korea).
Randomization and supplementation
In a double, blind, randomized trial, the subjects were
divided into placebo and treatment groups. The treatment
code was allocated randomly. To protect blinding, capsules
were packaged with identical labels containing an indi-
vidual unique randomization number. The randomization
number with treatment assignment for the individual sub-
ject was blinded for the duration of the trial. The subjects
received either two isoﬂavone or two placebo capsules
daily for 12 weeks. Each supplemented capsule contained
35 mg of isoﬂavone derived from soy germ. The total dose
of isoﬂavone was thus about 70 mg/day in glycoside,
which corresponded to 38.0 mg glycitin, 20 mg daidzin
and 12.4 mg genistin. Identical treatment and placebo
capsules were supplied by Dr. Chung’s Food Co. Ltd.
During the supplemental period, isoﬂavone intake from
foods was restricted to less than 10 mg/day. The subjects
received education on food sources of isoﬂavone by a
dietician.
General characteristics and anthropometric measures
The information on the general characteristics of the sub-
jects was collected through face to face interviews. The
anthropometric data were gathered using standard methods.
The body weight (kg) and height (cm) were measured to
the nearest 0.1 kg and 0.1 cm, respectively. The body mass
index (BMI) was calculated by dividing the body weight
(kg) by the squared height (m2). The waist and hip cir-
cumferences were measured twice with a ﬂexible steel
metric tape to the nearest 0.1 cm. The blood pressure (BP)
was measured twice with a sphygmomanometer (HM-
1101; HICO, Tokyo, Japan).
Assessment of dietary isoﬂavone intake
An experienced dietitian taught the subjects how to record
a food diary. Information on the subjects’ nutrient intakes
was collected through a 3-day diet record that included 2
weekdays and 1 day on the weekend. Isoﬂavone con-
sumption from foods was analyzed by CAN PRO 3.0 (The
Korean Nutrition Society, Seoul, Korea) (Franke et al.
1999; Lee et al. 2000).
Analysis of blood parameters
Blood was collected in the morning from a mid-arm vein
after overnight fasting (12 h). After the blood was centri-
fuged at 3,0009g at 4 C for 10 min, the supernatant was
stored at -80 C until it was assayed. The blood glucose
levels were analyzed using the enzymatic method (Bayer,
Japan). The serum total cholesterol (TC), triglyceride (TG),

123


and HDL-cholesterol (HDL-C) levels were analyzed using
the colorimetry method (Bayer, USA). The serum LDL-
cholesterol (LDL-C) levels were analyzed using the
enzyme immunoassay method (Bayer, USA). The serum
free fatty acid (FFA) levels were analyzed using the col-
orimetry method (HITACHI, Japan). The serum estrone
levels were analyzed via radioimmunoassay (PACKARD,
USA). The serum FSH, luteinizing hormone (LH), and
estradiol levels were analyzed via clinical laboratory
improvement amendments (Siemens, USA; estradiol: Ba-
yer, Japan).
Statistical analysis
Statistical analysis was performed using statistical analysis
software (SAS) version 9.1.3 (SAS Institute INC., Cary,
NC, USA). The categorical variables between the two
groups were compared with the chi-square test and the data
were presented as a percent or number. Also, continuous
variables between two groups or within a group were
compared with independent or paired t-test, respectively,
and data were presented as mean ± SD. Statistical signif-
icance was deﬁned at p \ 0.05.
Results
General characteristics
The general characteristics of the subjects are shown in
Table 1. The mean ages, menopausal period, medical his-
tory and using health functional foods were not different
between the groups.
Anthropometric measures
Anthropometric measures of the subjects are presented in
Table 2. Each variable of before and after intervention were
not signiﬁcantly different between the groups. The weights
of subjects in the placebo group were reduced after inter-
vention; however, the weight reductions were not signiﬁ-
cantly different between the groups (change of -0.5 ± 1.5
and 0.1 ± 1.0 kg, respectively). After the intervention,
waist to hip ratio (WHR) decreased signiﬁcantly in the
treatment group (-0.01 ± 0.03 changed); however, the
difference between the groups was not signiﬁcant Table 2.

The daily isoﬂavone intake is shown in Fig. 2. Before the
intervention, the daily consumption of isoﬂavone from foods
in the placebo and treatment groups was 16.8 ± 17.0 mg
(0.1–93.8 mg ranged) and 18.8 ± 14.2 mg (0.0–70.0 mg
ranged), respectively. After intervention, dietary isoﬂavone
consumption

total isoﬂavone consumption was about 74.0 mg per day due
to the 70 mg isoﬂavone supplement. The daily nutrients
intake is shown in Table 3. Although, the vitamin C and iron

treatment groups, respectively; however, no signiﬁcant dif-

HOMA-IR were not changed. For the lipid proﬁles, the
levels of TC, LDL-C and HDL-C were not changed after
intervention. However, TG levels in the treatment group

Discussion
This study explored the effects of supplementation of soy-
derived isoﬂavone on the blood glucose, lipid proﬁles and
sex hormones related to CVD in the Korean postmeno-
pausal women. We found that oral supplement of isoﬂav-
one for 12 weeks signiﬁcantly reduced serum levels of TG
and LH.
After menopause, the incidence of CVD increases fol-
lowing a decline in endogenous estrogen levels (Matthews
et al. 2001). Moreover, it is well recognized that meno-
pause is associated with alterations in body composition
such as a gain in abdominal fat mass, which increases
cardiovascular risks (Ferrara et al. 2002). Many studies

have explored exogenous estrogen treatment to improve
the condition of CVD in postmenopausal women. Pro-
spective cohort studies such as the Nurses’ Health Study
suggest that exogenous estrogen therapy decreases the risk
of coronary heart disease (CHD) in postmenopausal
women (Stampfer et al. 1991). Despite the prevalence of
ﬁndings that estrogen supported and even enhanced car-
diovascular function, data from large-scale clinical trials,
notably the WHI (WHI and WHI-CACS investigators
2007), indicated that postmenopausal women receiving
hormone replacement therapy (HRT) actually exhibited an
increase in the incidence of both CHD and stroke (WHI
investigators 2002; WHI Steering Committee 2004). The
use of HRT has thus become controversial, and it is nec-
essary to ﬁnd alternative strategies to reduce the risk of
CVD that could occur after menopause.
In October 1999, the US food and drug administration
(FDA) approved a health claim that products containing
soy protein are protective against CHD. This health claim
is based on the results of a clinical trial suggesting that at
least 25 g of soy protein per day reduced total-C and LDL-
C. However, the US FDA stated that ‘‘the evidence did not
support a signiﬁcant role for soy isoﬂavones in cholesterol-
lowering effects of soy protein.’’ Also, the AHA Nutrition
committee reevaluated the evidence on isoﬂavone and
CVD and updated its science advisory in 2006. They
reported that, among 19 studies of soy isoﬂavones, only 3
studies showed a reduction in LDL-C; however, no sig-
niﬁcant changes in HDL-C and TG were observed (Sacks
et al. 2006).

mentation with a soy protein containing isoﬂavones
signiﬁcantly reduced levels of TC, LDL-C and TG and
increased levels of HDL-C (Zhan and Ho 2005). In the case
of Asian subjects, treatment with 84 and 126 mg isoﬂavone
for 24 weeks had no effect on blood lipids in early post-
menopausal Chinese women (Ye et al. 2012).
In another RCT study in China, supplementation using
40 and 80 mg of isoﬂavone for 1 year showed no effects on
blood lipid proﬁle, however did show a reduction in fasting
glucose level. Interestingly, the isoﬂavone effects were
much more signiﬁcant among those that had a baseline
glucose level of 100 mg/dl or greater than in those with a
baseline glucose level of less than 90 mg/dl. (Ho et al.
2007). These results were dependent on the amount and
duration of isoﬂavone administration and the subject’s
condition related to CVD. Our results revealed that iso-
ﬂavone supplements (70 mg/day) for 12 weeks signiﬁ-
cantly reduced the levels of TG; however, other lipid
proﬁles and blood glucose levels were not affected by the
supplementation. It seems that because our subjects had
well-controlled blood glucose and lipid proﬁles, there
might be limited effects on these CVD related biomarkers.
In this study, the baseline dietary consumption of iso-
ﬂavones was 16.8–18.8 mg/day. This amount is similar to
that seen in a previous study (range of 18.5–20.9 mg/day)
with Korean postmenopausal women (Park et al. 2010;
Choi et al. 2005). Isoﬂavone consumption from foods is
different among the ethnic groups. In an earlier study,
dietary isoﬂavone consumptions of Chinese and Japanese
were 38.2 and 31.2 mg/day, respectively, whereas it was
only 6.8 mg/day for Caucasians and 5.0 mg/day for Fili-
pinos (Maskarinec et al. 1998).
Since the structure of isoﬂavone is very similar to that of
estrogen, it binds to estrogen receptors (ERs). Isoﬂavone
seems to have a higher afﬁnity for the ER-b receptor than
the ER-a receptor. It possesses dual effects, both estrogenic
and anti-estrogenic; however, whether it acts primarily as
an estrogen or as an anti-estrogen appears to depend on the
levels of circulating estrogens and types of ERs in indi-
viduals (Glazier and Bowman 2001).
A previous study found that supplementation of 60 mg/
day isoﬂavone signiﬁcantly increased estradiol (Petri et al.
2004). Duncan et al. 1999 showed reduction in estrone
values, with unchanged estradiol levels in menopausal
women on an isoﬂavone-rich diet. In other investigations,
no changes in hormonal levels were observed (Scambia
et al. 2000; Han et al. 2002). In the present study showed
that no changes of estrone and estradiol levels were
observed after similar dose of isoﬂavone supplements. This
discrepancy may be partly attributed, to the differences in
the amounts and/or duration of isoﬂavone supplements or
the subjects’ dietary soy consumption.
This study may have some weak points that the blood
levels of isoﬂavone and the activity levels of the subjects
were not measured. The strength of the study is that the
subjects were tightly controlled to consume similar amount
of dietary isoﬂavone.
In conclusion, supplementation with 70 mg/day of iso-
ﬂavone exerted favorable effect on the blood TG levels in
Korean postmenopausal women. Further studies are needed
to evaluate the clinical implication of these positive effects
in the postmenopausal women with CVD.
